summary: This informational memo describes scenarios for deploying IPv6 inside enterprise networks. It defines a small set of basic scenarios and includes questions to help administrators choose among them. It also discusses what enterprises require from IPv6 deployment.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4057 is a planning document for businesses that want to add IPv6 to their own network. It offers three broad shapes for that job, one for running both protocols side by side, one for adding IPv6 only where a few applications need it, and one for building an IPv6 network and keeping IPv4 for what still needs it. For each shape it lists the questions to answer first.

subtitle: Three shapes of IPv6 deployment for a business network, and the questions to answer before choosing one.

tldr.problem: An enterprise network team starting an IPv6 deployment has to pick a shape for it, and there was no shared set of cases to pick from, so every team invented its own and compared its results with nobody else's.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines three base scenarios, lists five groups of questions about the network infrastructure, and works through three example networks to show the range of situations a business might have.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo. It fixes no transition technique; it says the analysis of which coexistence mechanisms to use will come in a separate document.

today: RFC 4057 is an Informational memo published in June 2005, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets out scenarios for enterprise IPv6 deployment and says the analysis of the coexistence techniques and mechanisms to use will come in a separate document.

sections.title: Who This Document Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4057 describes scenarios for IPv6 deployment within enterprise networks. It defines a small set of basic enterprise scenarios and includes pertinent questions to allow enterprise administrators to refine their deployment scenarios further. Enterprise deployment requirements are discussed in terms of coexistence with IPv4 nodes, networks and applications, and in terms of basic network infrastructure requirements for IPv6 deployment. The scenarios and requirements described here are meant to be the basis for further analysis of what coexistence techniques and mechanisms are needed, and the results of that analysis will be published in a separate document.

The audience is the enterprise network team considering deployment of IPv6, and the document is expected to be useful to teams that will have to determine the transition strategy for their enterprise. Those teams are expected to include members from management, network operations and engineering. The scenarios presented provide an example set of cases that an enterprise can use to build an IPv6 network scenario.

It is impossible to define every possible enterprise scenario that will apply to IPv6 adoption and transition, and the memo is explicit that each enterprise will select the transition that best supports its business requirements. Any attempt to define a default or one-size-fits-all transition scenario simply will not work, and the document does not try to depict the drivers for adoption.

The document then reviews a set of network infrastructure components that must be analyzed and that are common to most enterprises, provides three specific scenario examples using those components to depict the requirements, and discusses the legacy functions that have to keep working while the transition is in process. Interoperation with legacy functions within the enterprise will be required for all transitions except possibly a new network that will be IPv6 from inception. The tools and mechanisms to support IPv6 deployment operations will require enterprise analysis, and the analysis of them is to be presented in subsequent documents.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a document for the people who have to decide how a business network moves to IPv6. Its argument is that there is no default answer: the right shape of deployment depends on the business, so the memo offers a set of cases to think with rather than a recipe to follow.

sections.title: The Words Used Here
sections.content:
The memo defines the terms it needs. An Enterprise Network is a network that has multiple internal links, one or more router connections to one or more Providers, and is actively managed by a network operations entity. A Provider is an entity that provides services and connectivity to the Internet or to other private external networks for the enterprise network.

A node or network is IPv6 Capable if it can support both IPv6 and IPv4. It is IPv4 only if it can support only IPv4, and IPv6 only if it can support only IPv6. The memo notes that the last term does not imply an IPv6-only stack in this document, meaning that a node called IPv6 only here may still carry other protocols below.

Elsewhere in the memo, network infrastructure means the software, the network operations and configuration, and the methods used to operate a network in an enterprise.
sections.plainLanguage: Three labels carry the whole document. A network is IPv6 capable if it can speak both protocols, IPv4 only if it can speak only the older one, and IPv6 only if it can speak only the newer one.

sections.title: The Three Base Scenarios
sections.content:
Three base scenarios are defined to capture the essential set of abstractions for the enterprise. Each has assumptions and requirements. The memo is clear that this is not an exhaustive set of scenarios but a base set of general cases, and that for the base scenarios it is assumed that any IPv6 node is IPv6 capable.

Scenario 1 is a wide-scale or total dual-stack deployment of IPv4 and IPv6 capable hosts and network infrastructure: an enterprise with an existing IPv4 network wants to deploy IPv6 in conjunction with its IPv4 network. The assumption is that the IPv4 network infrastructure used has an equivalent capability in IPv6. The requirements are to disrupt no existing IPv4 network infrastructure assumptions with IPv6, and for IPv6 to be equivalent or better than the network infrastructure in IPv4. It is understood that IPv6 is not required to solve current network infrastructure problems that IPv4 does not solve, and that it may not be feasible to deploy IPv6 on all parts of the network immediately.

Scenario 2 is a sparse IPv6 dual-stack deployment in IPv4 network infrastructure: an enterprise with an existing IPv4 network wants to deploy a set of particular IPv6 applications, and the deployment is limited to the minimum required to operate that set of applications. The memo notes that application is loosely defined here, giving peer-to-peer as an example. The assumptions are that IPv6 software and hardware components for the application are available and that the platforms for the application are IPv6 capable. The requirement is to disrupt no IPv4 infrastructure.

Scenario 3 is IPv6-only network infrastructure with some IPv4-capable nodes and applications needing to communicate over the IPv6 infrastructure: an enterprise deploying a new network, or restructuring an existing one, decides IPv6 is the basis for most network communication, while some IPv4-capable nodes and applications still need to talk over it. The assumption is that the required IPv6 network infrastructure is available, or available over some defined timeline, supporting the enterprise plan. The requirement is that interoperation and coexistence with IPv4 network infrastructure and applications are required for communications.

Section 3.2 then sets out five groups of questions that the enterprise must answer. The first group, enterprise provider requirements, asks whether external connectivity is required, whether there is one site or several and whether they are in different geographies, whether leased lines or VPNs are used, how traffic between multiple sites is exchanged securely, how many global IPv4 addresses are available, what IPv6 address assignment plan the provider offers, what prefix delegation is required, whether the enterprise will be multihomed and what multihoming techniques the provider offers, whether clients inside the enterprise will be multihomed, whether the provider offers any IPv6 services, which site-external IPv6 routing protocols are required, whether there is an external data centre, and whether IPv6 is available on the same access links as IPv4 or on different ones. The second group, enterprise application requirements, asks which applications are in use, which must be moved to IPv6 first, whether they can be upgraded, whether they will have to support both protocols, whether the platforms support both, whether the applications have issues with NAT, whether they need globally routable addresses, whether they care about a dependency between IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and whether they run only on the internal network. The third group, enterprise IT department requirements, asks who owns and operates the network, whether working remotely through VPNs is supported, whether inter-site communication is required, whether network mobility is used, what the IPv6 address plan requires, whether there is a detailed asset management database, how geographically separate sites with their own service providers are to be numbered, what the internal IPv6 address assignment procedure will be, what site-internal IPv6 routing protocols are required, what the IPv6 network management, QoS and security policies will be, what the IPv6 training plan is, and which network operations software and hardware will be affected by IPv6 and whether those can be upgraded. The fourth group, the enterprise network management system, asks about performance management, network management applications, configuration management, policy management and enforcement, security management, management of the transition tools and mechanisms, and what new considerations IPv6 creates for network management. The fifth group, interoperation and coexistence, asks which platforms have to be IPv6 capable, which ingress and egress points to the site have to be IPv6 capable, what transition mechanisms are needed, and what policies and procedures are needed for the transition and for interoperation with legacy nodes and applications.

The applicability statement at the end of the section says the examples are a base set and not a complete set of network scenarios. Example Network C is a verifiable use case, but it describes an early adopter moving to IPv6 as the predominant protocol and treating IPv4 as legacy operations immediately in the transition strategy, and at the time it may not be representative of many initial enterprise IPv6 deployments. Each enterprise planning team will have to make that determination as IPv6 deployment evolves.
sections.plainLanguage: The three shapes are: run both protocols everywhere, add IPv6 in the few places a particular application needs it, or make IPv6 the main network and keep IPv4 for what still has to work over it. After the shapes come the questions, grouped by who has to answer them: the provider, the applications, the IT department, the network management people, and the coexistence work.

sections.title: Three Example Networks
sections.content:
The memo then works through three example networks, chosen to show the range of situations an enterprise might have. The examples may use the scenarios and infrastructure components described earlier, but there are no direct implications within them, and the earlier sections are to be used in unison with these for planning and analysis.

Example Network A is a distributed network across a number of geographically separated campuses. External network operation is used, external connectivity is required, multiple sites are connected by leased lines, IPv4 addresses are provider independent, the ISP does not offer IPv6 service, and there is no service provider on the private leased lines. The enterprise runs internal web and mail, file servers, Java applications, collaborative development tools, enterprise resource applications, multimedia applications, financial enterprise applications and data warehousing applications. The network is operated in house. DHCP version 4 is used for all desktops while servers use static address configuration, the DHCP server that updates naming records for dynamic desktops uses dynamic DNS, a web-based tool is used to enter name to address mappings for statically addressed servers, and network management is done with SNMP. All routers and switches are upgradeable to IPv6 and the existing firewalls can be upgraded to support IPv6 rules, but the load balancers do not support IPv6 and their upgrade path is unclear. Peer-to-peer application and security are supported, and private IPv4 address space is used within the enterprise.

Example Network B is a bank running a large network supporting online transaction processing across a distributed multi-sited network, with access to a central database on a remote network from the online transaction processing network. External connectivity is not required. Multiple sites are connected by VPN and by native IP protocol. Private address space is used with NAT, and there are connections to private exchanges. The applications are an ATM transaction application, an ATM management application, and financial software and database, and part of the workforce is mobile and requires access to the enterprise from outside networks. The existing firewalls can be upgraded to support IPv6 rules, the load balancers do not support IPv6 and their upgrade path is unclear, and identifying and managing each node's IP address is a concern.

Example Network C is a security, defence, emergency or other mission critical network operation. External network is required at secure specific points, the network is its own Internet, it must be able to absorb the ad-hoc creation of sub-networks, and entire parts of the network are completely mobile, with all nodes on the network able to be mobile, including routers. High availability is mandatory, the network must be able to be managed from an ad-hoc location, and all nodes must be able to be configured from stateless mode. The applications include multimedia streaming of audio, video and data for all nodes, data computation and analysis on stored and created data, transfer of data coordinate points to sensor devices, and data and intelligence gathering applications from all nodes. All packets must be secured end to end with encryption, intrusion detection exists on all network entry points, the network must be able to bolt on to the Internet to share bandwidth as required from providers, VPNs can be used but NAT can never be used, and nodes must be able to access IPv4 legacy applications over the IPv6 network.
sections.plainLanguage: The three examples are deliberately different. One is a company spread over several campuses with leased lines between them. One is a bank running transaction processing across sites with its own database elsewhere. One is a mobile, mission critical network that has to be its own Internet and must never use address translation.

sections.title: The Infrastructure to Check
sections.content:
The enterprise will need to determine which network infrastructure components require enhancements or need to be added for IPv6 deployment. The list is not exhaustive, but it contains the essential components to consider before defining more fine-tuned requirements such as QoS, PKI or bandwidth requirements. The components are only identified here and their details will be discussed in the analysis document.

DNS has to support both IPv4 and IPv6 records, and the enterprise has to work out how the DNS is managed, accessed and secured. The range of DNS operational issues is beyond the scope of the document, but DNS resolution and transport solutions for both IP protocols are influenced by the chosen deployment scenario, so users need to consider all current DNS IPv4 operations and determine whether those operations are supported for IPv6.

Routing will have to support both IPv4 and IPv6 protocols and the coexistence of the two over the enterprise network. The enterprise has to define the IPv6 routing topology, any ingress and egress points to provider networks, and the transition mechanisms it wants to use, and to determine which transition mechanisms its upstream providers support.

Configuration of hosts gains a new option, because IPv6 introduces stateless autoconfiguration in addition to stateful autoconfiguration. The enterprise has to decide which method of host configuration to use, how autoconfiguration will operate for DNS updates, how prefix delegation will be done from the upstream provider, and how those prefixes will be cascaded down to the enterprise IPv6 network. The policy for DNS or the choice of autoconfiguration is out of scope.

Security has to keep working: the mechanisms used for IPv4 to provide security need to be supported for IPv6 within the enterprise, and IPv6 should create no new security concerns for IPv4. The entire security infrastructure in use has to be analyzed against the effect of IPv6 deployment, and users will have to work with their platform and software providers to find out which components are supported. The security filters and firewall requirements for IPv6 have to be determined by the enterprise.

Applications will need to be ported or provide proxies to support both IPv4 and IPv6. Network management for the new IPv6 components will be run by the enterprise network operations centre, and users will need to work with their network management platform providers to find out what is supported for IPv6 and which tools are available to monitor the network. The memo notes that network management will not need to support both IPv4 and IPv6 and view nodes as dual stacks. Address planning has to define the address space within the enterprise and coordinate it with the routing topology; it is also important to identify the pool of IPv4 address space available to the enterprise, to assist with IPv6 transition methods. Multicast users of IPv4 multicast services will need to consider how those services may be implemented operationally in an IPv6-enabled environment. Multihoming is constrained by current IPv6 allocation policies, which mandate allocation of IPv6 address space from the upstream provider, so a multihomed enterprise has to determine how it wishes to support multihoming; the memo notes that this is also an area of study within the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: Nine things have to be checked before the deployment plan is written: name resolution, routing, how machines get their addresses, security, the applications, the management system, the address plan, multicast, and being connected to more than one provider. Most of them are the same jobs the enterprise already does for IPv4, and the question is whether the tooling can do them twice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it lists scenarios for the deployment of IPv6 in enterprise networks, and that there are no security considerations associated with making such a list. It then adds that there will be security considerations for the deployment of IPv6 in each of these scenarios, but that they will be addressed in the document that includes the analysis of each scenario.
sections.plainLanguage: Listing scenarios raises no security questions of its own. The security questions belong to each scenario, and the memo says they are handled in the analysis document that follows.

items.title: Scenario 1: dual stack
items.text: An enterprise with an existing IPv4 network deploys IPv6 in conjunction with it, across IPv6 capable hosts and infrastructure. Do not disrupt the IPv4 assumptions, and make IPv6 equivalent or better.

items.title: Scenario 2: sparse
items.text: An enterprise deploys a set of particular IPv6 applications, and the deployment is limited to the minimum needed to run them. Do not disrupt the IPv4 infrastructure.

items.title: Scenario 3: IPv6 primary
items.text: A new or restructured network makes IPv6 the basis for most communication, while some IPv4-capable nodes and applications still have to communicate over it. Coexistence is required.

cells: The network is its own Internet
Provider independent IPv4 addresses, private inside
Load balancers do not support IPv6
Part of the workforce is mobile
All packets secured end to end

items.title: DNS
items.text: Support both IPv4 and IPv6 records, and decide how the DNS is managed, accessed and secured.

items.title: Routing
items.text: Support both protocols and their coexistence, define the IPv6 topology and ingress and egress points, and check what upstream providers support.

items.title: Host configuration
items.text: Choose stateless or stateful autoconfiguration, decide how it works with DNS updates, and plan prefix delegation from the provider.

items.title: Security
items.text: Support the mechanisms used for IPv4, and determine the security filters and firewall requirements for IPv6.

items.title: Applications
items.text: Existing applications will need to be ported or provide proxies to support both IPv4 and IPv6.

items.title: Network management
items.text: Work out what the management platform supports for IPv6 and which tools are available to monitor the network.

items.title: Address planning
items.text: Define the enterprise address space, coordinate it with the routing topology, and identify the pool of IPv4 addresses available to help with transition.

items.title: Multicast and multihoming
items.text: Decide how IPv4 multicast services map into an IPv6-enabled environment, and how a multihomed enterprise wants to support multihoming.
